exam: Explain how impaired oxidative phosphorylation leads to lactic acidosis in septic shock.
List three common drug classes that cause mitochondrial toxicity and describe their clinical presentation.
Interpret a lactate of 6 mmol/L with a normal PaO2 in a patient with fever and hypotension.
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Bioenergetics studies how cells produce, store, and use energy. It links metabolism to clinical states like shock, sepsis, and mitochondrial disease, guiding diagnosis and treatment.

b: ATP is the universal energy currency.
Mitochondria are the powerhouses where OXPHOS occurs.
Anaerobic glycolysis yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
sections.p: Cells obtain energy mainly from oxidation of glucose, fatty acids, and amino acids via glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). ATP generated powers all cellular functions.

b: ATP demand rises in fever, tachycardia, and tissue repair.
Supply falls with hypoxia, mitochondrial toxins, or nutrient deficiency.
The NADH/FADH2 pool links substrate oxidation to the electron transport chain.
sections.p: Understanding the balance between ATP supply and demand explains many acute and chronic illnesses.

t.b: Is there anaerobic metabolism? High lactate indicates inadequate OXPHOS, seen in shock or mitochondrial failure.
Is tissue oxygenation sufficient? Low PaO2 or high A‑a gradient suggests impaired oxidative phosphorylation.
Is glycolysis up‑regulated? Elevated ratio supports mitochondrial dysfunction.

b: Septic shock: mitochondrial inhibition → high lactate, refractory hypotension.
Ischemic stroke: ATP depletion → cell death within minutes.
Mitochondrial myopathy: exercise intolerance, elevated CK, normal lactate at rest.
sections.p: Disrupted bioenergetics manifests as lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia, or organ failure. Recognising patterns directs urgent care.

b: Lactate >2 mmol/L signals anaerobic metabolism; >4 mmol/L in sepsis predicts higher mortality.
Inherited mitochondrial disease often shows ragged‑red fibers on muscle biopsy.
Hypoglycemia with normal insulin suggests increased peripheral utilization (e.g., sepsis).
sections.p: Focus on cause‑effect relationships and diagnostic thresholds.

b: Assuming normal lactate rules out shock – early shock may have normal lactate.
Ignoring drug‑induced mitochondrial toxicity (e.g., linezolid, antiretrovirals).
Attributing fatigue solely to anemia without assessing ATP production.
sections.p: Avoid oversimplifying energy failure as only ‘low oxygen’. Consider substrate, enzyme, and cofactor deficits.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe lactic acidosis (lactate >5 mmol/L) with hypotension
Rapidly falling glucose <2.5 mmol/L in a non‑diabetic patient
Acute unexplained encephalopathy with metabolic acidosis
